subtitulo: Short, and why short is the polite one
introPt: A traveller drops the cushions, orders in five words, and gets served at the speed the counter actually runs.
cenario: A busy counter mid-morning, the machine going, three people behind you.

dialogo.es: Αμέσως. Για εδώ ή για έξω;
dialogo.pt: Right away. For here or to take away?
dialogo.tts: Αμέσως. Για εδώ ή για έξω;

perguntas.pergunta: Someone at a counter says «Παρακαλώ;» to you. It means:
perguntas.explica: Parakaló does four jobs. Said to you with a rise on the end at a counter, it opens your turn.

perguntas.pergunta: Politeness research places Greek and English on which sides?
opcoes: Greek on closeness and involvement, English on distance and non-imposition
Greek on distance, English on closeness
perguntas.explica: Positive politeness on the Greek side, negative politeness on the English side. The misreading runs in both directions and is symmetrical.

perguntas.pergunta: Your long, heavily hedged English request tends to land as:
opcoes: Distance — the opposite of what you meant
perguntas.explica: The cushions read as holding yourself back. Move the courtesy to the greeting and to parakaló, and let the middle be two words.

perguntas.pergunta: The price list at a Greek counter is:
opcoes: Optional, and asking for it is rude
Compulsory in Greek, visible at the entrance and before you order, prices including VAT
perguntas.explica: Under the ΔΙ.Ε.Π.Π.Υ. rules, with a €1,000 fine for its absence and €500 per item charged above it. Reading it on the way in is its ordinary use.

perguntas.pergunta: Which is the well-shaped counter order?
opcoes: A long apology, then the request, then another apology
The thing on its own, with no greeting
perguntas.explica: Greeting, then the thing, then parakaló. Short in the middle, courteous at both edges — and never skip the greeting.
